title: 49ers are to Blame for Mike Evans' Achilles Injury - Sports Illustrated
description:
He left Monday night’s game against the Commanders right before halftime with an Achilles injury and wouldn’t return.
Anytime a player leaves a game with an Achilles injury, it causes panic.
Evans’ injury is twofold.
The 49ers deserve blame for Evans’ Achilles injury.
Evans didn’t take part in a single practice in the lead-up to Monday night against the Commanders because of Achilles soreness.
text:
Mike Evans was expectedly held out of the 49ers’ first Week 7 practice against the Falcons.

He left Monday night’s game against the Commanders right before halftime with an Achilles injury and wouldn’t return. Anytime a player leaves a game with an Achilles injury, it causes panic.

Thankfully, Evans didn’t suffer a season-ending Achilles tear. But he is experiencing tendinitis. It would be very surprising if Evans plays this week against the Falcons, especially with the Bye week after.

Evans’ injury is twofold. On one hand, it’s a sigh of relief that Evans didn’t tear his Achilles. On the other hand, he shouldn’t have gotten hurt against the Commanders because he shouldn’t have played.

The 49ers deserve blame for Evans’ Achilles injury. Evans didn’t take part in a single practice in the lead-up to Monday night against the Commanders because of Achilles soreness.

That should’ve been a red flag to the 49ers. They, of all teams, should know how serious Achilles injuries are, even if it’s just soreness. It happened two years ago with Christian McCaffrey.

You’d think they’d learn that it’s best to be extremely cautious with a player who’s dealing with any Achilles-related issue. Instead, they allowed Evans to play because he wanted to. They failed to protect him from himself.

“Mike's got a lot of experience doing this stuff,” Kyle Shanahan said in Monday night’s postgame. “Mike's pretty honest with us too, and my life experiences with him over six games, if he says he's ready to go, I believe him.”

Believing in Evans is foolish. What NFL star doesn’t want to play, no matter how they’re feeling? Evans isn’t thinking about the consequences and risks of playing through Achilles soreness.

All that matters to him is playing and helping his team. That’s how tough he is, but he doesn’t need to prove anything to anyone. What he needs is someone to hold him out from worsening his injury.

The 49ers failed to prevent that because Evans wanted to play. They let him play that game as if it were against the Seahawks in December, with the NFC West on the line.

Now, they have to rely on Jordan Watkins, Jacob Cowing, and a newly signed Brandin Cooks. The wide receiver position was already razor-thin.

It's desolate now, and it opens the floodgates for 49ers fans to pound the table for a wide receiver trade. This all could've been avoided if they had sat him against the Commanders.

What a blunder.

text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- The Kansas City Chiefs placed left tackle Josh Simmons on injured reserve Thursday, further delaying his return from a bulging, herniated disk in his lower back.

After being a limited participant in the Chiefs' three practices last week, Simmons still felt pain in his back and left leg, the same leg he had previously suffered a torn patellar tendon in back in October 2024 while playing for Ohio State.

Head trainer Rick Burkholder shared Thursday that Simmons reported feeling discomfort in his left calf following a training camp practice Aug. 17, prompting the team to order an MRI, which revealed a "bulging, herniated" disk, he said.

"That disk problem was higher up than what we normally see in most of our offensive linemen, which complicated the case," Burkholder said of Simmons. "The repeat MRI, a few weeks later, showed that the disk had improved, so no surgery was recommended. Josh worked his tail off. He worked diligently with my staff every day. However, we feel he has plateaued in the rehab process. He's just not there yet."

Burkholder then explained that Simmons took the rest of Wednesday afternoon off to discuss the next steps of his treatment with his family and his representative, thus the "personal" and "back" designations on the Chiefs' injury report.

According to Burkholder, "everybody" agreed that Simmons needed to be placed on injured reserve, a move that will force the lineman to miss at least the next four games -- against Seattle, Denver, the New York Jets and Atlanta. The earliest Simmons can return is Week 11, when the Chiefs host the Arizona Cardinals on Nov. 22.

The team and Simmons are still determining how and where he will continue his rehab.

"I give a lot of credit to Josh, my physicians and my staff for navigating through this injury to the point where surgery is not recommended," Burkholder added. "He just needs more time to return to full function."

Simmons' absence has opened the door for undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson, who played right tackle in college for the Indiana Hoosiers. Benson is the first undrafted offensive rookie to start in Week 1 for Andy Reid during his entire 14-year coaching tenure in Kansas City. Benson has done a commendable job as the lineman most responsible for protecting the blind side of quarterback Patrick Mahomes, earning NFL Offensive Rookie of the Month in September.

On the other side, right tackle Jaylon Moore, a five-year veteran, is currently in the NFL's concussion protocol. Joshua Ezeudu, who joined the Chiefs in late August via a trade with the New York Giants, is expected to start in Moore's place in Sunday night's road game against the Seahawks.

Since selecting Simmons in the first round of the 2025 NFL draft, the Chiefs have played more games without him (14) than with him (eight). The last time Simmons played was last year on Thanksgiving Day, when the team fell to the Dallas Cowboys. During that game, Simmons suffered a dislocated and fractured left wrist, a season-ending injury that required surgery. Before that setback, Simmons was an emerging rookie, as he allowed a pressure rate of just 6.6%, which at the time was the third-lowest mark among left tackles and the second lowest by a rookie left tackle since 2018 (minimum 150 pass blocks), according to Next Gen Stats.

"His job is to make sure that he's physically getting himself ready for what's next," offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy said Thursday of Simmons "He's just got to focus one day at a time."
